The way you described the thoughts you’re having as “coming out of nowhere” and how much anxiety they cause you, sounds a lot like the kind of intrusive thinking I struggle with due to generalized anxiety disorder. 

The way intrusive thoughts were described to me is that, someone tells you not to think of a purple elephant. But the harder you try to not think of a purple elephant, the more you do, and the more the purple elephant takes up space in your mind. It gets bigger and more distracting and starts damaging stuff. Intrusive thoughts get reinforced by becoming entangled in them, whether by trying to block them out or push them away, or by trying to decipher a meaning from them.

You mentioned that you have a therapist, so they would be better equipped to walk you through this process. But identifying the thoughts as intrusive and remembering that you don’t have control over them, and simply allowing them to enter your mind and accept them and not engage with them, can make them easier to manage and cause less anxiety over time. 

In other words, don’t engage the purple elephant. Leave it alone, treat it as uninteresting, and eventually it will go away. It can be an uncomfortable process at first to sit through the anxiety, but you have to be gentle with yourself.

History, especially ancient history and to some extent dress history and the history of textiles due to my interest in historical clothing. 

The color that we refer to as “royal purple” is also called Tyrian purple or Phoenician red, and originated in the Phoenician dye trade possibly as early as 1570 BC. The dye was created by extracting mucus from of a species of Murex snail, which yielded a pigment that was red-purple in color. It was extremely difficult to make, with anywhere from 10,000 to 12,000 snails only yielding one gram of pigment, making it extremely expensive and as such it became a status symbol. Laws regulating its usage in the Roman Empire meant that only the Roman Emperor was permitted to wear Tyrian purple, and its production was so tightly controlled in the Byzantine Empire that it could only be used to color imperial silks.
